## Scope

This guide covers the transition to OrgPath for an estate with a specific and
common shape:

- **one Active Directory forest containing multiple domain trees** — several
  distinct DNS namespaces under one schema and one Global Catalog;
- **one live Entra ID tenant** at the GCC-Moderate boundary; and
- **directory synchronisation already established**, so every user in the
  tenant is a synced object rather than a cloud-only one.

The worked estate below is twelve trees in one forest. Nothing in the sequencing
depends on the number; substitute your own tree count and the phase structure is
unchanged.

It complements rather than repeats the canon material. The pattern — attributes
plus dynamic groups plus Administrative Units replacing the OU tree — is
[UIAO_007](../../reference-architecture/orgtree.qmd). The step-by-step runbook is
UIAO_156. The phase model is
[ADR-081](../../../adr/adr-081-directory-migration-phase-canonical-model.qmd).
What none of those state is the **sequencing constraint a fully-synced estate
imposes**, which is what this guide exists for.

## 1. What the estate shape decides for you

Three properties of the shape settle three questions that would otherwise be
open design decisions. They are worth stating explicitly, because each one
closes off an approach that looks reasonable in the abstract.

### 1.1 One forest means discovery is cheap

Multiple trees in a *single* forest share one schema, one Configuration naming
context, one Global Catalog, and transitive two-way trusts throughout. For
OrgPath purposes the estate is closer to one large directory than to N
directories.

Concretely, a single `GC://<forest-root>` query enumerates principals across
every tree. The per-forest service accounts and two-way-trust prerequisite
documented for genuinely multi-*forest* estates in
[Windows Server Deployment](../../platform/windows-server-deployment.qmd) do not
apply here.

Multiple trees still matter — for UPN suffix routing, GPO scoping, delegated
administration boundaries, and the order of decommissioning — but not for the
cost of discovery.

### 1.2 Every user being synced decides the write path

This is the constraint that shapes everything downstream.

For a **directory-synced** user, `onPremisesExtensionAttributes` is **read-only
in the cloud**. The OrgPath facets cannot be stamped directly onto those objects
through Graph. They must be written **on-premises in Active Directory** and
carried up by sync.

Canon already assumes this. [ADR-063](../../../adr/adr-063-orgpath-storage-slot-binding.qmd)
rejects that slot family for cloud-only tenants precisely because the attributes
are *"replicated from on-prem AD via Entra Connect and are read-only in the
cloud,"* and the Active Directory survey adapter is specified to write *"OrgPath
back to extensionAttributes in AD for Entra Connect pickup."*

The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it inverts the intuition that
a cloud-forward programme writes to the cloud:

> During the overlay, the AD forest is the **write path**. It stops being the
> *source* of organisational truth on day one — that becomes HR — but it remains
> the *transport* for OrgPath until the sourcing cutover.

Two corollaries:

- **Do not mirror the forest into an external LDAP copy.** A copy is a
  point-in-time snapshot that freezes current drift, and it loses even the thin
  history AD does keep, since replication metadata
  (`msDS-ReplAttributeMetaData`, `msDS-ReplValueMetaData`) is constructed and does
  not survive an LDIF export. The forest you would be copying is the one you still
  need to write to.
- **The device plane is a separate surface.** Device `extensionAttributes` are
  writable through Graph regardless of join type, so the device plane
  ([ADR-038](../../../adr/adr-038-device-plane-orgpath.qmd)) does not carry this
  constraint. Expect the user plane and device plane to have *different* write
  paths during coexistence.

### 1.3 A live tenant means there is no tenant migration

The overlay target already exists. Every principal across all trees is already a
cloud object with a settled source anchor.

Standing up a second production tenant would convert an in-place
attribute-stamping exercise into a full tenant-to-tenant migration — mailboxes,
device re-enrolment, app registrations, Conditional Access baselines, licensing,
B2B relationships — and would require re-anchoring the estate, which is among the
least forgiving operations in Entra. None of that is required by the OrgPath
model, which stamps facets and a derived path onto objects that already exist.

A **pre-production** tenant remains correct and is assumed by canon: UAT-1 and
UAT-2 run against a pre-prod tenant. Build one to rehearse stamping, rule
evaluation, and AU delegation — not as the production destination.

## 2. The sequencing constraint

Canon's steady-state posture is **cloud-first and asymmetric**: Entra is source
of truth, AD-side edits are unsupported, and a writeback configuration carries a
defined attribute set back down for residual on-premises consumers.

That posture is **post-cutover**. It cannot run on day one against a
fully-synced estate, because §1.2 forbids the cloud-side write it depends on.
The transition therefore has two stages, and conflating them is the most likely
way to design a pipeline that silently does nothing:

| Stage | Source of truth | OrgPath written to | Reaches Entra via |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Overlay** (from day one) | HR | On-premises AD | Directory sync |
| **Steady state** (post-cutover) | Entra | Entra | Writeback to AD for legacy consumers |

The event that separates them is the **sourcing cutover** — §5.

## 3. Prerequisites

Three checks gate the programme. All three are cheap; none should be assumed.

### 3.1 Do the extension attributes exist in the schema?

`extensionAttribute1`–`15` arrive with the Exchange schema extension
(`ms-Exch-Extension-Attribute-N`). One forest means one schema, so this is a
single yes/no for the whole estate.

If the answer is no, a **forest-wide schema extension becomes a gating change
window** with its own approval path — a materially different programme start
than if the attributes are already present.

### 3.2 Are the target slots already occupied?

ADR-063 §3 requires a formal rebind procedure when a non-OrgPath value already
occupies a target slot for a non-trivial population (defined as ≥1% of in-scope
users):

1. snapshot existing values to the Evidence Fabric with a `DRIFT-PROVENANCE`
   annotation, preserving the prior investment for audit;
2. identify the inherited use — typically a cost-centre, location code, or
   mailbox-region tag — and record the prior owner; then
3. negotiate a relocation slot before any OrgPath write occurs.

Across a dozen trees, expect at least one to have colonised these slots
independently. Run the occupancy census **per tree**, not forest-wide in
aggregate: a 0.4% forest-wide occupancy can still be 100% of one tree.

### 3.3 How do the UPN suffixes route?

Multiple trees means multiple DNS namespaces and potentially multiple UPN
suffixes. With sync already established this is usually settled, but confirm
whether each suffix is a verified tenant domain or whether some trees' users
landed on an alternate suffix.

This does not affect OrgPath. It shapes the **decommission sequence**, so it is
worth knowing before you plan §6 rather than during it.

## 4. Phase map

The canon six-phase model applies unchanged. What follows is where a multi-tree,
fully-synced estate diverges from the generic reading.

| Canon phase | Applied to this estate |
|---|---|
| **Discover** | One `GC://<forest-root>` sweep across all trees, plus per-tree GPO, delegation, and LDAP-bind inventories. Slot-occupancy census per §3.2. |
| **Normalize** | Build the governed OrgTree **from HR**, explicitly independent of the current OU layout. |
| **Map** | Produce the AD-versus-HR delta (§4.1). Map each legacy OU to facet values against the codebook; flag unmappable OUs for governance review. |
| **Migrate** | Stamp facets and the derived path **into AD**, per tree, in waves. Sync carries them up. |
| **Validate** | Confirm facets landed on the cloud objects; build OrgPath-keyed dynamic groups and AUs; re-base policy targeting so governance stops reading OU position. |
| **Decommission** | Per tree, after its own soak. Twelve gates — §6. |

### 4.1 The delta is the deliverable

The highest-value artefact this programme produces is not the stamped attribute.
It is the **reconciliation between what the twelve trees assert and what HR
asserts**.

The OU estate is a downstream projection of organisational truth that has drifted
across years of reorganisations, mergers, and ad-hoc container moves. OrgTree is
seeded from HR precisely because the OU tree is no longer a reliable statement of
the organisation. That makes the delta a governance finding in its own right —
frequently the first defensible, evidence-backed statement of how far the
directory has diverged from the organisation it was built to model.

Treat the twelve-tree structure as a **mapping input and a drift report**, never
as a source.

### 4.2 What is overlaid, and what is retired

The transition does **not** realign the OU tree to match reality. OU remediation
as a standalone project is expensive, high-risk, and obsoleted by the overlay:
once policy reads OrgPath, the OU tree's correctness stops being a governance
signal.

That is not licence to ignore OU-bound dependencies. Group Policy links,
delegated administration, and LDAP-bound applications are inventoried in the
dependency map and retired deliberately. Every LDAP-dependent application should
land in exactly one of the four canonical target states — application proxy,
SAML, OIDC, or a managed domain service — before the tree hosting it is retired.
An application with no documented target state is a decommission blocker, and it
is better to discover that in Discover than in Decommission.

## 5. The cutover is a sourcing flip, not a tenant move

There is a real cutover date, and it is worth naming precisely because
"cutover" invites the wrong mental model.

It is the moment **Entra becomes source of truth**: AD-side edits stop being
supported, on-premises write access is constrained at the ACL layer to a service
identity plus a small break-glass set, and writeback begins carrying attributes
down to whatever legacy consumers remain. The production cutover runbook covers
the sequence; the validation report gates entry to it.

What it is **not** is a migration of objects between tenants. Nothing moves. The
same objects, in the same tenant, change which system is authoritative for them.

Two practical notes:

- **One cutover, twelve retirements.** The sourcing flip is estate-wide. Tree
  retirement is not.
- **The risk lives in the coexistence window, not on the date.** A long
  coexistence period with both planes writable is where drift accumulates. The
  posture that AD-side edits are unsupported must be *enforced*, not merely
  documented, or the next sync silently overwrites an operator's change with no
  warning.

## 6. Decommission: twelve gates, not one date

Each tree retires on its own evidence. The canon Decommission phase exists
precisely so that retirement follows validation rather than coinciding with it,
and the customer guides in adjacent domains set the expectation for soak periods:
the DNS modernisation guide requires a 30-day validation window followed by 90
days of parallel operation before retiring legacy servers; the PKI guide holds a
30-day rollback window before its Decommission phase.

Apply the same discipline per tree. A tree is retirable when:

1. every principal in it carries validated facets and a derived path;
2. no policy, group, or AU still targets it by OU position;
3. every GPO, delegation, and LDAP-bound application it hosted has a documented
   target state that has been executed;
4. its soak has elapsed with no critical drift events; and
5. the retirement is signed off and recorded.

Sequence the trees by dependency and blast radius, not by convenience. The tree
carrying the forest root and its FSMO roles retires **last**, and its retirement
is a separate exercise from retiring a leaf tree.

## What this guide does not decide

Stated explicitly so the boundaries are not mistaken for omissions:

- **It does not choose your HR integration.** The architecture binds to no
  specific HR product; the source slot is a property of the deployed vertical.
- **It does not size the waves.** Wave composition depends on tree size,
  business calendar, and help-desk capacity — none of which the estate shape
  determines.
- **It does not cover mainframe or non-Windows directory consumers**, which
  follow their own adapter paths.
- **It does not address a genuinely multi-forest estate.** If a second forest
  exists, §1.1 no longer holds and discovery reverts to the per-forest model.
